meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid empirical contributions (systematic characterization of cross-forum domain shift, honest reporting of negative results, dataset release) but has significant methodological limitations and conceptual ambiguities that should be addressed. The core contribution—identifying 'fine-grained domains' within cybercrime forums—is interesting but undermined by lack of formal definition and reliance on correlational rather than causal evidence. The paper would be substantially strengthened by: (1) formally defining 'fine-grained domains' with explicit criteria or operationalization; (2) comparing to neural sequence models and neural domain adaptation methods to establish whether negative results reflect method limitations or fundamental task difficulty; (3) directly measuring stylistic/contextual differences between forums rather than inferring them from performance patterns; (4) controlling for confounding variables (e.g., dataset size) when comparing source domains; (5) applying multiple-comparison correction to statistical significance tests; (6) providing detailed analysis of annotation disagreement patterns and discussing implications for ground truth reliability. The paper's honest reporting of negative results and systematic empirical characterization are valuable, but the contribution is primarily empirical characterization rather than methodological innovation. The work is suitable for publication as a resource contribution with empirical characterization of a specific problem, but should not be oversold as introducing a fundamentally new concept or solving the domain adaptation problem. The paper would be most valuable for researchers working on cybercrime marketplace analysis and for those interested in understanding limitations of standard domain adaptation methods on noisy, specialized text.
meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes valuable contributions through systematic empirical characterization and honest reporting of negative results. To strengthen the work, address the following concerns: (1) Define 'fine-grained domains' formally—either operationally (e.g., 'forums with <X% product inventory overlap') or theoretically. Without formal definition, the core concept remains vague and difficult to generalize. (2) Explore stronger baselines: compare to neural sequence models (BiLSTM-CRF) and neural domain adaptation methods (adversarial training, transfer learning). This will clarify whether marginal improvements from standard methods reflect method limitations or fundamental task difficulty. (3) Directly measure stylistic differences: compute linguistic features (vocabulary overlap, syntactic patterns, discourse markers) and correlate with performance degradation. This moves from correlational to causal analysis. (4) Control for confounding variables: when claiming Darkode is 'more general', control for dataset size by subsampling Hack Forums to match Darkode size. (5) Apply multiple-comparison correction: use Bonferroni or FDR control for the ~20 statistical tests in Tables 3-4. (6) Analyze annotation disagreement: provide detailed breakdown of which product types or contexts cause disagreement, and discuss implications for ground truth reliability. (7) Clarify post-level accuracy claims: emphasize that ~95% accuracy applies only to within-forum Darkode setting; cross-forum accuracy is substantially lower (67.6%). (8) Discuss dataset availability: commit to specific timeline for release, address ethical/legal considerations for cybercrime data, and provide detailed annotation guidelines to enable reproducibility even if full dataset cannot be released. (9) Reframe hypotheses: present inventory and stylistic factors as complementary rather than alternative, and quantify their relative contributions. (10) Acknowledge limitations: explicitly discuss generalizability concerns (only 4 forums, cybercrime domain only) and discuss how findings might extend to other domains.

epistemic_limits: Generalizability: Only 4 forums tested; findings may not extend to other cybercrime forums or other domains with internal heterogeneity. The concept of 'fine-grained domains' may be specific to marketplace forums or cybercrime domain.

Causal inference: Analysis of domain differences is correlational; stylistic/contextual factors are inferred from performance patterns rather than directly measured. Causal attribution requires experimental manipulation or more sophisticated causal inference methods.

Ground truth reliability: Moderate inter-annotator agreement (0.58-0.77 Kappa) and small annotated subset (2.1% of posts) raise questions about representativeness and reliability of ground truth labels. Majority voting may suppress legitimate annotation ambiguity.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This hybrid empirical-methodological paper presents a dataset of 93,924 posts from 4 cybercrime forums with 1,938 annotated posts, a task formulation for product identification as a hybrid of slot-filling IE and NER, and systematic evaluation of domain adaptation techniques. The core claim is that cybercrime forums constitute distinct 'fine-grained domains' causing severe cross-forum performance degradation (14.4 F1 drop: 63.2 vs 77.6), and that standard domain adaptation methods (Brown clusters, gazetteers, Daume III) provide only marginal improvements (0.5-1.5 F1 points). The paper's strength lies in honest reporting of negative results and systematic empirical characterization of cross-forum domain shift. However, the contribution is undermined by: (1) lack of formal definition for the central concept 'fine-grained domains'; (2) correlational rather than causal analysis of domain differences; (3) moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77) and small annotated subset (2.1%) raising ground truth reliability concerns; (4) uncorrected multiple comparisons in statistical testing; (5) hand-crafted SVM baseline without neural sequence model comparisons; (6) limited generalizability (only 4 forums, cybercrime domain only). The paper opens a potentially valuable research direction but requires substantial methodological strengthening to support its claims.
strengths: Systematic empirical characterization of cross-forum domain shift with multiple evaluation metrics (token-level, phrase-level, type-level, post-level) and clear quantification of performance degradation (14.4 F1 drop)
Honest reporting of negative results: explicitly acknowledges that standard domain adaptation methods provide only marginal improvements, preventing wasted effort on ineffective approaches

Transparent annotation methodology with inter-annotator agreement reporting (Fleiss' Kappa 0.58-0.77 for all forums) and documented annotation process (6 preliminary rounds, majority voting for training, discussion-based resolution for dev/test)
Multi-faceted evaluation metrics reflecting task complexity and different application requirements (token-level for detailed analysis, post-level for practical applications)
Dataset release with substantial annotation effort (1,938 annotated posts across 4 forums) enabling future research on cybercrime marketplace analysis
Asymmetric adaptation analysis revealing source domain properties: observation that Hack Forums→Darkode adaptation works better than reverse, connected to OOV rates and product coverage differences
Task formulation bridging IE and NER with context-dependent product identification (only products in transaction context), novel for marketplace forums
limitations: Core concept 'fine-grained domains' lacks formal definition despite being central to the contribution. The paper never specifies what distinguishes 'fine-grained' from 'coarse-grained' domain shift, or what properties define a fine-grained domain. This undermines the conceptual contribution and limits generalizability to other domains.

Moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77 across forums) raises ground truth reliability concerns. Agreement values in the 0.58-0.77 range are typically considered 'moderate' rather than 'substantial', suggesting non-trivial disagreement that may not be fully resolved by majority voting (for training) or discussion-based resolution (for dev/test). The paper does not analyze disagreement patterns or discuss implications for model training and evaluation.

Statistical significance testing lacks multiple-comparison correction. With approximately 20 statistical tests across Tables 3-4 using bootstrap resampling with p<0.05 threshold, the false positive rate is likely inflated (expected false positive rate ≈ 1 - (0.95)^20 ≈ 64%). This undermines confidence in claimed improvements from domain adaptation methods.

Causal attribution of domain differences is correlational rather than experimental. The analysis infers stylistic/contextual factors from asymmetric adaptation performance and OOV rates, but does not directly measure stylistic features or conduct experimental manipulation. The claim that 'stylistic conventions play a significant role' (line 750) is speculative.

Hand-crafted SVM features may not be optimal baseline for domain adaptation evaluation. The paper does not compare to neural sequence models (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF) or more recent neural domain adaptation approaches (adversarial training, transfer learning). This limits the strength of negative results about adaptation method effectiveness.

Only 2.1% of posts are annotated (1,938/93,924), raising representativeness concerns. The paper does not describe the sampling strategy for annotated posts or analyze whether the annotated subset differs from the full dataset in terms of post length, product frequency, or other characteristics.

Generalizability limited by small sample size: only 4 forums tested (Darkode, Hack Forums, Blackhat with only 80 annotated posts, Nulled). Unclear whether fine-grained domain effects generalize to other cybercrime forums or other domains with internal heterogeneity.

Confounding variable in source domain comparison: Darkode's better OOV performance (21% vs 41-52% for other forums) may reflect its larger training set (3,368 posts) rather than inherent generality. The paper does not control for dataset size when comparing source domains.
open_questions: What formally distinguishes 'fine-grained domains' from standard domain adaptation challenges? The paper uses this term throughout but never provides a formal definition. Is it based on product inventory overlap, stylistic similarity, or some other metric? How would practitioners operationalize this concept for new domains?

Why do standard domain adaptation methods (Brown clusters, gazetteers, Daume III) provide only marginal improvements? Is this due to: (a) fundamental task difficulty, (b) suboptimal hyperparameter tuning, (c) weak baseline (hand-crafted SVM features), or (d) the specific characteristics of cybercrime forum data? How would results change with neural sequence models or more recent neural domain adaptation approaches?

What are the relative contributions of product inventory differences (Hypothesis 1) vs. stylistic/contextual differences (Hypothesis 2) to cross-forum performance degradation? The paper presents these as alternatives but the analysis suggests both contribute. Can you quantify their relative importance (e.g., via regression analysis or ablation studies)?

How reliable is the ground truth given moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77)? What types of products or contexts cause disagreement? How sensitive are the results to different annotation resolution strategies (e.g., strict agreement vs. lenient agreement)?

Do the findings generalize beyond the 4 forums tested? Would fine-grained domain effects be observed in other cybercrime forums (e.g., AlphaBay, Dream Market) or in other domains with internal heterogeneity (e.g., product reviews across categories, scientific papers across subfields)?

Why does Darkode-trained system have lower OOV rates across all target forums? Is this due to: (a) inherent product coverage differences, (b) larger training set (3,368 posts), or (c) different product vocabulary distribution? How would results change if you controlled for training set size?

How much of the cross-forum performance degradation is due to annotation quality differences vs. true domain shift? Different annotation procedures for train (majority vote) vs. dev/test (discussion-based resolution) could introduce systematic differences. Have you analyzed this?

What is the practical applicability of the post-level formulation given substantial cross-forum degradation (95.8% within-forum vs. 67.6% cross-forum for Hack Forums→Darkode)? For which applications is this level of degradation acceptable?
consensus_snapshot: Cross-forum performance degradation is substantial and well-documented: 14.4 F1 drop (63.2 vs 77.6) for Hack Forums→Darkode on NP-level evaluation
Standard domain adaptation techniques provide only marginal improvements: 0.5-1.5 F1 points with many improvements not statistically significant
Product inventory differences (OOV rates: 21-44% across forums) partially explain cross-forum degradation, but other factors also contribute

Different annotation procedures for train (majority vote) vs. dev/test (discussion-based resolution) are documented, but potential systematic differences are not analyzed.

The paper acknowledges limitations ('these results do not tell the full story', line 791) but lacks transparency in several areas: no sampling strategy for annotated posts, no parser error analysis, no discussion of confounding variables, no exploration of stronger baselines.

The paper promises dataset and code release 'upon publication', but actual availability is contingent on publication decision and author willingness to share. No timeline or commitment to long-term availability provided.

The paper does not provide sufficient detail about hyperparameter selection for domain adaptation methods (e.g., why 50 Brown clusters, why 4-occurrence gazetteer threshold), limiting reproducibility of negative results.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid empirical contributions through systematic characterization of cross-forum domain shift and honest reporting of negative results. The work is suitable for publication as a resource contribution with empirical characterization of a specific problem, but requires substantial methodological strengthening to support its claims. Key recommendations: (1) Formally define 'fine-grained domains' with explicit criteria or operationalization—this is central to the contribution but currently vague. (2) Compare to neural sequence models (BiLSTM-CRF) and neural domain adaptation methods to establish whether negative results reflect method limitations or fundamental task difficulty. (3) Apply multiple-comparison correction to statistical significance tests (Bonferroni or FDR control). (4) Directly measure stylistic/contextual differences between forums rather than inferring from performance patterns. (5) Control for confounding variables (e.g., dataset size) when comparing source domains. (6) Provide detailed analysis of annotation disagreement patterns and implications for ground truth reliability. (7) Acknowledge generalizability limitations (only 4 forums, cybercrime domain only) and discuss how findings might extend to other domains. The paper's honest reporting of negative results and systematic empirical characterization are valuable, but the contribution is primarily empirical characterization rather than methodological innovation. The work would be most valuable for researchers working on cybercrime marketplace analysis and those interested in understanding limitations of standard domain adaptation methods on noisy, specialized text.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Your paper makes valuable contributions through systematic empirical characterization and honest reporting of negative results. To strengthen the work, address these key concerns: (1) Define 'fine-grained domains' formally—either operationally (e.g., 'forums with <X% product inventory overlap') or theoretically. Without formal definition, the core concept remains vague. (2) Explore stronger baselines: compare to neural sequence models (BiLSTM-CRF) and neural domain adaptation methods (adversarial training, transfer learning). This clarifies whether marginal improvements reflect method limitations or fundamental task difficulty. (3) Directly measure stylistic differences: compute linguistic features (vocabulary overlap, syntactic patterns, discourse markers) and correlate with performance degradation. This moves from correlational to causal analysis. (4) Control for confounding variables: when claiming Darkode is 'more general', control for dataset size by subsampling Hack Forums to match Darkode size. (5) Apply multiple-comparison correction: use Bonferroni or FDR control for the ~20 statistical tests in Tables 3-4. (6) Analyze annotation disagreement: provide detailed breakdown of which product types or contexts cause disagreement, and discuss implications for ground truth reliability. (7) Clarify post-level accuracy claims: emphasize that ~95% accuracy applies only to within-forum Darkode setting; cross-forum accuracy is substantially lower (67.6%). (8) Discuss dataset availability: commit to specific timeline for release, address ethical/legal considerations for cybercrime data, and provide detailed annotation guidelines to enable reproducibility. (9) Reframe hypotheses: present inventory and stylistic factors as complementary rather than alternative, and quantify their relative contributions. (10) Acknowledge limitations: explicitly discuss generalizability concerns (only 4 forums, cybercrime domain only) and discuss how findings might extend to other domains.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This hybrid empirical-methodological paper presents a dataset of 93,924 posts from 4 cybercrime forums with 1,938 annotated posts, a task formulation for product identification as a hybrid of slot-filling IE and NER, and systematic evaluation of domain adaptation techniques. The core claim is that cybercrime forums constitute distinct 'fine-grained domains' causing severe cross-forum performance degradation (14.4 F1 drop), and that standard domain adaptation methods provide only marginal improvements (0.5-1.5 F1 points). The paper's strength lies in honest reporting of negative results and systematic empirical characterization. However, the contribution is undermined by lack of formal definition for 'fine-grained domains', correlational rather than causal analysis, moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77), uncorrected multiple comparisons, and limited generalizability (only 4 forums).

Strengths:
- Systematic empirical characterization of cross-forum domain shift with multiple evaluation metrics (token-level, phrase-level, type-level, post-level) and clear quantification of performance degradation (14.4 F1 drop)
- Honest reporting of negative results: explicitly acknowledges that standard domain adaptation methods provide only marginal improvements, preventing wasted effort on ineffective approaches
- Transparent annotation methodology with inter-annotator agreement reporting (Fleiss' Kappa 0.58-0.77 for all forums) and documented annotation process (6 preliminary rounds, majority voting for training, discussion-based resolution for dev/test)
- Multi-faceted evaluation metrics reflecting task complexity and different application requirements (token-level for detailed analysis, post-level for practical applications)
- Dataset release with substantial annotation effort (1,938 annotated posts across 4 forums) enabling future research on cybercrime marketplace analysis
- Asymmetric adaptation analysis revealing source domain properties: observation that Hack Forums→Darkode adaptation works better than reverse, connected to OOV rates and product coverage differences
- Task formulation bridging IE and NER with context-dependent product identification, novel for marketplace forums

Limitations:
- Core concept 'fine-grained domains' lacks formal definition despite being central to the contribution. The paper never specifies what distinguishes 'fine-grained' from 'coarse-grained' domain shift, or what properties define a fine-grained domain. This undermines the conceptual contribution and limits generalizability to other domains.
- Moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77 across forums) raises ground truth reliability concerns. Agreement values in the 0.58-0.77 range are typically considered 'moderate' rather than 'substantial', suggesting non-trivial disagreement that may not be fully resolved by majority voting (for training) or discussion-based resolution (for dev/test). The paper does not analyze disagreement patterns or discuss implications for model training and evaluation.
- Statistical significance testing lacks multiple-comparison correction. With approximately 20 statistical tests across Tables 3-4 using bootstrap resampling with p<0.05 threshold, the false positive rate is likely inflated. This undermines confidence in claimed improvements from domain adaptation methods.
- Causal attribution of domain differences is correlational rather than experimental. The analysis infers stylistic/contextual factors from asymmetric adaptation performance and OOV rates, but does not directly measure stylistic features or conduct experimental manipulation. The claim that 'stylistic conventions play a significant role' is speculative.
- Hand-crafted SVM features may not be optimal baseline for domain adaptation evaluation. The paper does not compare to neural sequence models (CRF, BiLSTM-CRF) or more recent neural domain adaptation approaches. This limits the strength of negative results about adaptation method effectiveness.

Open Questions:
- What formally distinguishes 'fine-grained domains' from standard domain adaptation challenges? The paper uses this term throughout but never provides a formal definition. Is it based on product inventory overlap, stylistic similarity, or some other metric?
- Why do standard domain adaptation methods provide only marginal improvements? Is this due to: (a) fundamental task difficulty, (b) suboptimal hyperparameter tuning, (c) weak baseline (hand-crafted SVM features), or (d) specific characteristics of cybercrime forum data? How would results change with neural sequence models?
- What are the relative contributions of product inventory differences (Hypothesis 1) vs. stylistic/contextual differences (Hypothesis 2) to cross-forum performance degradation? The paper presents these as alternatives but the analysis suggests both contribute. Can you quantify their relative importance?
- How reliable is the ground truth given moderate inter-annotator agreement (Kappa 0.58-0.77)? What types of products or contexts cause disagreement? How sensitive are the results to different annotation resolution strategies?
- Do the findings generalize beyond the 4 forums tested? Would fine-grained domain effects be observed in other cybercrime forums or in other domains with internal heterogeneity?

Transparency:
The paper is transparent about inter-annotator agreement and explicitly reports marginal improvements from standard domain adaptation methods, demonstrating scientific integrity. However, the paper lacks transparency in several areas: no sampling strategy for annotated posts, no parser error analysis, no discussion of confounding variables (e.g., dataset size differences), no exploration of stronger baselines. The paper promises dataset and code release 'upon publication', but actual availability is contingent on publication decision. The paper does not discuss ethical considerations for releasing cybercrime forum data.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: ✅ TASK 2. Assignment check
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, policy_screen
Content: s. If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission, your review should specify that, and you will also be able to indicate your confidence score in the ARR form. The good news is that the less-than-perfect matches also have upsides: you get to expand your repertoire, the authors get feedback on what needs more clarification/explanation, and NLP in general gets more intellectual exchange between subfields. The second thing to check is whether you know or can guess who the authors are. Ideally, ARR peer review should be fully anonymous. The problem with implicit social biases is that they are unconscious; we may be 100% sure that we do not think worse of a paper just because it is written by someone from a group minoritized in computing research and that we are not predisposed to like papers coming from famous labs, but we cannot really trust our conscious selves. If you happen to know who the authors are from personal communication, social media or talks, the review form will contain a field for you to indicate whether you know who the authors are. If you believe that some case is particularly bad and may severely compromise your judgement (e.g. because of a conflict of interest (COI): you know the authors personally, have or will work with them, etc.), please ask your AC for re-assignment if possible. If you feel that you are qualified to review some aspects of the paper but not others (e.g. experimental results but not the formal proofs), please state in the review if you did not check some major parts, such as proofs.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: ✅ TASK 2. Assignment check
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, policy_screen
Content: s. If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission, your review should specify that, and you will also be able to indicate your confidence score in the ARR form. The good news is that the less-than-perfect matches also have upsides: you get to expand your repertoire, the authors get feedback on what needs more clarification/explanation, and NLP in general gets more intellectual exchange between subfields. The second thing to check is whether you know or can guess who the authors are. Ideally, ARR peer review should be fully anonymous. The problem with implicit social biases is that they are unconscious; we may be 100% sure that we do not think worse of a paper just because it is written by someone from a group minoritized in computing research and that we are not predisposed to like papers coming from famous labs, but we cannot really trust our conscious selves. If you happen to know who the authors are from personal communication, social media or talks, the review form will contain a field for you to indicate whether you know who the authors are. If you believe that some case is particularly bad and may severely compromise your judgement (e.g. because of a conflict of interest (COI): you know the authors personally, have or will work with them, etc.), please ask your AC for re-assignment if possible. If you feel that you are qualified to review some aspects of the paper but not others (e.g. experimental results but not the formal proofs), please state in the review if you did not check some major parts, such as proofs.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
